## Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

Organizing means matching storage location to an item's meaning. A seamless system allows your mind to let go of lower-level thinking. Airtight organization is required for focus on the broader horizon and eliminating pressure to remember. The system will evolve as you process your "stuff" and test placements.

### The Basic Categories
Seven primary categories manage commitments:
*   A Projects list
*   Project support material
*   Calendar actions and information
*   Next Actions lists
*   A Waiting For list
*   Reference material
*   A Someday/Maybe list

**The Importance of Hard Edges:** Categories must be kept pristinely distinct visually, physically, and psychologically. Blending causes psychological numbness (e.g., reference mixed with unread items, non-calendar items on the calendar, Someday/Maybe items on the Projects list, Waiting For items on action lists). Capturing and clarifying your relationship to items is primary.

**All You Really Need Are Lists and Folders:** Lists (groupings of items with similar characteristics) and folders (digital or paper) are sufficient tools. Lists can be: (1) a file folder/container with separate notes, (2) a titled list on paper, or (3) a digital list. Avoid imposing external priority scaffolding on lists; they are inventories for review, not daily prioritizing guides. Prioritizing happens intuitively against shifting variables during review.

### Organizing Action Reminders
Pending reminders (longer-than-two-minute, non-delegated actions) need sorting into reviewable groupings.

**The Actions That Go on Your Calendar:** Only "hard landscape" items belong here: time-specific ("10:00–11:00 meet with Jim") or day-specific ("Call Rachel Tuesday"). Resist putting aspirational "to-do" items here; trust the calendar as sacred territory reflecting exact commitments. Most actions fall into "as soon as possible."

**Organizing As-Soon-As-Possible Actions by Context:** The best way to be reminded of ASAP actions is by the context required (tool, location, situation). Discreteness depends on (1) number of actions and (2) frequency of context changes. A single list suffices for ~25 actions; more require context lists to avoid unproductive re-sorting. Context lists leverage energy when in a specific mode (e.g., "phone mode").

**The Most Common Categories of Action Reminders:**
*   **Calls:** All phone calls. Include phone numbers. Useful for mobile windows of time.
*   **At Computer:** Actions requiring a computer. Consider separating "Online" (requires internet) if relevant (e.g., Allen maintains separate "At Computer" and "Online" lists for flights). Location-specific lists (e.g., At Office, At Home) might incorporate computer work.
*   **Errands:** Actions done when out and about (e.g., "Get stock certificates from bank deposit box," "Pick up suit at tailor," "Buy flowers for Robyn"). Track sublists within items (e.g., "hardware store" with appended items). Location-based reminders are a useful *addition* to rigorously managed lists, not a replacement.
*   **At Office:** Actions requiring physical presence in the office (e.g., purging a filing cabinet). Relevant if you have separate Calls/At Computer lists. May need sublists for multiple locations (e.g., At Office "A" and "B").
*   **At Home:** Actions only doable at home (e.g., "Hang new watercolor print," "Organize travel accessories," "Switch closets to winter clothes"). Includes home office actions if you work from home.
*   **Anywhere:** Actions doable in any context.
*   **Agendas:** Items to cover with specific people or in specific meetings. Keep separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children, attorneys, financial advisers, standing meetings (staff, project, board, committee). Create ad hoc lists for temporary interactions (e.g., a contractor). System should allow quick addition.
*   **Read/Review:** Longer-than-two-minute reading/viewing. Manage physically in a tray/folder ("Read/Review"). Critical to keep this pile pristine and only for desired items to avoid numbness. Consider "Review/Respond" for rigorous reading. Useful for leveraging waiting times. Digital equivalents (e.g., "Review/Watch" email folder, "Surf Web" list) manage online content.

**Organizing “Waiting For”:** Track deliverables or projects others are responsible for (e.g., theater tickets, scanner delivery, client proposal approval). Your role is to review the list and assess if action (e.g., status check) is needed. Keep close to Next Actions lists as responsibility bounces. Include the date requested and any due date for effective follow-up. A complete inventory provides relief and improved focus.

**Using the Original Item as Its Own Action Reminder:** Often efficient to use the originating trigger (paper, email) as the reminder instead of writing a list item, especially for:
*   **Paper-Based Workflow:** Read/Review materials, Bills to Pay, Receipts to Process. Danger: Must be reviewed consistently. Organize by next action required (e.g., Calls, At Computer), not just document type.
*   **E-mail-Based Workflow:** Actionable emails can be stored in the email system. Set up folders prefixed (e.g., "@") to sort top: "@ACTION" (longer-than-two-minute actionable emails), "@WAITING FOR" (emails indicating someone will do something you care about, delegated requests). Getting "In" to empty means deleting, filing reference, doing <2 min, and moving actionable/waiting items to these folders. "@ACTION" is an extension of At Computer and must be reviewed equally.

**A Caution About Dispersing Reminders:** Distributing triggers is OK *only if* all categories are reviewed equally as required. Digital reminders can "disappear" off-screen, reducing trust; physicality can increase trust. System must allow quick review of all actionable items.

### Organizing Project Reminders
**The Projects List(s):** A comprehensive index of *all* open loops (commitments/desired outcomes requiring >1 action step). Not for plans/details, not arranged by priority/size/urgency. You work off action lists/calendar, not the Projects list directly. Its real value lies in the complete review (at least weekly) ensuring action steps are defined for all projects and nothing slips through cracks. A complete list is the major operational tool for moving from "tree-hugging to forest management."

**The Value of a Complete Projects List:** Critical for control/focus, alleviates subtle tensions (small things morphing into bigger things), core of the Weekly Review, facilitates relationship management (negotiating resource allocation).

**Where to Look for Projects Still to Uncover:**
*   **Current Activities:** Calendar items (meetings, trips), action list items (e.g., "Call Mario re: fund-raising event" implies project "Finalize the fund-raiser"), workspace artifacts (proposals, forms, broken watch).
*   **Higher-Horizon Interests/Commitments:** Review professional accountabilities, roles, goals, objectives, strategic plans, personal life areas (kids, parents, retirement, partner's aspirations, creative interests).
*   **Current Problems, Issues, Opportunities:**
    *   *Problems:* Always projects (e.g., "Look into improving Frederick’s relationship with his school," "Resolve situation with landlord," "Get closure on compensation dispute").
    *   *Process Improvements:* Frustrations with systems/procedures (filing, communication, hiring, expense reporting, banking, keeping in touch).
    *   *Creative/Capacity-Building Opportunities:* "Might like to" learn/experience things (e.g., learn Italian cooking, take a digital photography course). May start on Someday/Maybe but can become Projects.

**One List, or Subdivided?** One list is usually best as a master inventory. Review all contents as often as needed (usually in Weekly Review). Subsorting options:
*   *Personal/Professional:* Comfort for some, but review both judiciously.
*   *Delegated Projects:* For senior managers tracking projects handed off to reports.
*   *Specific Types of Projects:* E.g., "Projects—Presentations" for a trainer, "Sales Relationships in Progress" for an agent.
*   *Areas of Focus:* E.g., by children, by entrepreneurial roles (Finance, Sales, Operations).

**What About Subprojects?** Large projects (e.g., "Move to Amsterdam") may have major subprojects (e.g., "Set up Dutch bank accounts," "Finalize artwork storage"). Options: (1) List the large project on Projects list, keep subprojects in support material (reviewed during Weekly Review), especially if dependent; (2) List active, independent subprojects separately. No perfect system; ensure you know where all moving parts are and review frequently. (Allen example: "Move to Amsterdam" unpacked into 15 projects as it became immediate).

**Project Support Materials:** Resources supporting actions/thinking, *not* reminders. **Don't Use Support Material for Reminding:** Using stacks/files/emails as reminders leaves next actions psychologically embedded, creating subliminal pressure and numbness. First, add the project to the Projects list. Then define action steps/Waiting For items for action lists. Pull support materials only when *doing* an action or during Weekly Review. Store plans/overviews accessibly if not disciplined to review files weekly.

**Organizing Ad Hoc Project Thinking:** Capture ideas about projects/topics. Methods:
*   *Attached Notes:* Use digital notes attached to list/calendar entries or Post-its on paper lists.
*   *E-mail and Software Applications:* Dedicated email folders (e.g., "Johnson Partnership—Active"), digital databases, note-taking software, project management tools. Danger: Spreading info too widely loses coordination; maintain a clear Projects list and scan regularly.
*   *Paper-Based Files:* Separate folders for projects; print digital items for physical reference during interactions.
*   *Pages in Notebooks:* Dedicate pages/groups to projects in loose-leaf notebooks. Clear out inactive/redundant notes.

### Organizing Nonactionable Data
Blending actionable and nonactionable items clogs the system. Nonactionable categories: Reference, Someday/Maybe, Trash.

**Reference Materials:** Information with no action required, kept for various reasons. Decisions: how much to keep, storage space, form, location. Once distinguished from actionable items, it's just your library; volume adds no psychological weight if system is clean.

**The Variety of Reference Systems:**
*   *General-Reference Filing:* Paper, email, simple digital storage. Must be informal, accessible, easy to file/retrieve. Needs 1-4 physical drawers, many digital folders.
*   *Large-Category Filing:* Topics needing >50 folders/major documents get dedicated sections/drawers/databases (e.g., corporate merger docs, hobby files). Stick to one general system except for discrete topics.
*   *Contact Managers:* Pure reference (phone numbers, emails, details). Problem arises if used for action reminders instead of action lists. Logistics of access are key.
*   *Libraries and Archives:* Personalized levels based on need/access (mobile device, briefcase, office files, departmental archives, cloud, web). Logistical/purpose-based organization. No "perfect" system; build from managing day-to-day realities.

**Someday/Maybes:** Items to reassess later (e.g., "Learn Spanish," "Get Marcie a horse," "Climb Mt. Washington," "Write a mystery novel," "Get a vacation cottage"). Not throwaway; potentially creative.

**Someday/Maybe List:** Create and populate. Sources: creative imagination (e.g., things to get/build, hobbies, skills, creative expressions, clothes, toys, trips, organizations, service projects, things to see/do) and reassessing current projects (move optional projects here if no attention for months). Subcategorize if useful (e.g., home projects vs. bucket list fantasies, parking lot ideas vs. capital-dependent projects).

**Special Categories of Someday/Maybe:** Lists for specific interests (e.g., Food—recipes/restaurants, Children—activities, Books to read, Music to download, Movies to see, Gift ideas, Web sites to explore, Weekend trips, Ideas—Misc.). Cross between reference and Someday/Maybe.

**The Danger of “Hold and Review” Files and Piles:** Not recommended. People hold but don't review, leading to numbness/resistance. Often contains items needing toss, Read/Review, reference filing, calendar/tickler, or actual next actions. Value disappears without conscious review.

**Using the Calendar for Future Options:** Use day-specific slots for reminders to reassess later:
*   *Triggers for Activating Projects:* Future dates for projects needing lead time (e.g., product launches, fund-raisers), regular events (budget reviews, annual conferences), key dates (birthdays, anniversaries).
*   *Events You Might Want to Participate In:* Put a trigger closer to the event date (e.g., "Check out XYZ conference" 2 months prior).
*   *Decision Catalysts:* For significant decisions needing delay (e.g., hire/fire, merge/acquire/sell/divest, change job/career, strategy redirection). "It’s OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system."

**The “Tickler” File:** A 3D calendar (43 folders: 31 daily "1"-"31", 12 monthly). Physical reminders "mail" themselves to your in-tray on a future date. Setup: Daily files for next 31 days in front, followed by next month's file, then remaining daily files for current month, then remaining monthly files. Empty daily file into in-tray daily, refile at back of dailies (now representing next month). Empty monthly file into in-tray when it reaches front, refile at back of monthlies (now representing that month next year). Requires daily check/update. Advantage: Stores actual documents. Represents "deciding not to decide until a certain point."

### Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders
Checklists ("recipes of potential ingredients") provide reminders for projects, processes, events, areas of responsibility. They extend the number of operations performed without thinking (Whitehead). Entrust details to your "external mind."

**Things You Want to Pay Attention To:** Fuzzy internal commitments (e.g., "Exercise more regularly," "Maintain good morale on my team," "Focus more on spiritual practices").

**First, Identify Inherent Projects and Action:** Translate fuzzier items into projects/actions (e.g., "Exercise more regularly" -> Project: "Set up regular exercise program"; Action: "Call Sally for suggestion about gyms"). Some items need checklists instead.

**Blueprinting Key Areas of Work and Accountability:** Overview checklists for key areas (e.g., Career goals, Service, Family, Relationships, Community, Health, Financial resources, Creative expression; within job: Team morale, Processes, Timelines, Staff issues). Value is affirming areas are OK or need change.

**The More Novel the Situation, the More Control Required:** Unfamiliarity demands external checklists (e.g., prescribed procedures, new software, new job responsibilities). Use until familiar (e.g., checklist of new responsibilities during business restructuring).

**Checklists at All Levels:** Create any checklist as needed (e.g., "Core Life Values," "Things to Take Camping," "Potential Holiday Gifts," "Job Areas of Responsibility," "Exercise Regimens," "Travel Checklist," "Weekly Review," "Training Program Components," "Key Clients," "People to Stay in Touch With," "Year-end Activities," "Personal Development," "Jokes"). Capability to instantly make and use accessible checklists is core to high-performance self-management.

*   *Personal/Professional:* Comfort for some, but review both judiciously.
*   *Delegated Projects:* For senior managers tracking projects handed off to reports.
*   *Specific Types of Projects:* E.g., "Projects—Presentations" for a trainer, "Sales Relationships in Progress" for an agent.
*   *Areas of Focus:* E.g., by children, by entrepreneurial roles (Finance, Sales, Operations).

**What About Subprojects?** Large projects (e.g., "Move to Amsterdam") may have major subprojects (e.g., "Set up Dutch bank accounts," "Finalize artwork storage"). Options: (1) List the large project on Projects list, keep subprojects in support material (reviewed during Weekly Review), especially if dependent; (2) List active, independent subprojects separately. No perfect system; ensure you know where all moving parts are and review frequently. (Allen example: "Move to Amsterdam" unpacked into 15 projects as it became immediate).

**Project Support Materials:** Resources supporting actions/thinking, *not* reminders. **Don't Use Support Material for Reminding:** Using stacks/files/emails as reminders leaves next actions psychologically embedded, creating subliminal pressure and numbness. First, add the project to the Projects list. Then define action steps/Waiting For items for action lists. Pull support materials only when *doing* an action or during Weekly Review. Store plans/overviews accessibly if not disciplined to review files weekly.

**Organizing Ad Hoc Project Thinking:** Capture ideas about projects/topics. Methods:
*   *Attached Notes:* Use digital notes attached to list/calendar entries or Post-its on paper lists.
*   *E-mail and Software Applications:* Dedicated email folders (e.g., "Johnson Partnership—Active"), digital databases, note-taking software, project management tools. Danger: Spreading info too widely loses coordination; maintain a clear Projects list and scan regularly.
*   *Paper-Based Files:* Separate folders for projects; print digital items for physical reference during interactions.
*   *Pages in Notebooks:* Dedicate pages/groups to projects in loose-leaf notebooks. Clear out inactive/redundant notes.

### Organizing Nonactionable Data
Blending actionable and nonactionable items clogs the system. Nonactionable categories: Reference, Someday/Maybe, Trash.

**Reference Materials:** Information with no action required, kept for various reasons. Decisions: how much to keep, storage space, form, location. Once distinguished from actionable items, it's just your library; volume adds no psychological weight if system is clean.

**The Variety of Reference Systems:**
*   *General-Reference Filing:* Paper, email, simple digital storage. Must be informal, accessible, easy to file/retrieve. Needs 1-4 physical drawers, many digital folders.
*   *Large-Category Filing:* Topics needing >50 folders/major documents get dedicated sections/drawers/databases (e.g., corporate merger docs, hobby files). Stick to one general system except for discrete topics.
*   *Contact Managers:* Pure reference (phone numbers, emails, details). Problem arises if used for action reminders instead of action lists. Logistics of access are key.
*   *Libraries and Archives:* Personalized levels based on need/access (mobile device, briefcase, office files, departmental archives, cloud, web). Logistical/purpose-based organization. No "perfect" system; build from managing day-to-day realities.

**Someday/Maybes:** Items to reassess later (e.g., "Learn Spanish," "Get Marcie a horse," "Climb Mt. Washington," "Write a mystery novel," "Get a vacation cottage"). Not throwaway; potentially creative.

**Someday/Maybe List:** Create and populate. Sources: creative imagination (e.g., things to get/build, hobbies, skills, creative expressions, clothes, toys, trips, organizations, service projects, things to see/do) and reassessing current projects (move optional projects here if no attention for months). Subcategorize if useful (e.g., home projects vs. bucket list fantasies, parking lot ideas vs. capital-dependent projects).

**Special Categories of Someday/Maybe:** Lists for specific interests (e.g., Food—recipes/restaurants, Children—activities, Books to read, Music to download, Movies to see, Gift ideas, Web sites to explore, Weekend trips, Ideas—Misc.). Cross between reference and Someday/Maybe.

**The Danger of “Hold and Review” Files and Piles:** Not recommended. People hold but don't review, leading to numbness/resistance. Often contains items needing toss, Read/Review, reference filing, calendar/tickler, or actual next actions. Value disappears without conscious review.

**Using the Calendar for Future Options:** Use day-specific slots for reminders to reassess later:
*   *Triggers for Activating Projects:* Future dates for projects needing lead time (e.g., product launches, fund-raisers), regular events (budget reviews, annual conferences), key dates (birthdays, anniversaries).
*   *Events You Might Want to Participate In:* Put a trigger closer to the event date (e.g., "Check out XYZ conference" 2 months prior).
*   *Decision Catalysts:* For significant decisions needing delay (e.g., hire/fire, merge/acquire/sell/divest, change job/career, strategy redirection). "It’s OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system."

**The “Tickler” File:** A 3D calendar (43 folders: 31 daily "1"-"31", 12 monthly). Physical reminders "mail" themselves to your in-tray on a future date. Setup: Daily files for next 31 days in front, followed by next month's file, then remaining daily files for current month, then remaining monthly files. Empty daily file into in-tray daily, refile at back of dailies (now representing next month). Empty monthly file into in-tray when it reaches front, refile at back of monthlies (now representing that month next year). Requires daily check/update. Advantage: Stores actual documents. Represents "deciding not to decide until a certain point."

### Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders
Checklists ("recipes of potential ingredients") provide reminders for projects, processes, events, areas of responsibility. They extend the number of operations performed without thinking (Whitehead). Entrust details to your "external mind."

**Things You Want to Pay Attention To:** Fuzzy internal commitments (e.g., "Exercise more regularly," "Maintain good morale on my team," "Focus more on spiritual practices").

**First, Identify Inherent Projects and Action:** Translate fuzzier items into projects/actions (e.g., "Exercise more regularly" -> Project: "Set up regular exercise program"; Action: "Call Sally for suggestion about gyms"). Some items need checklists instead.

**Blueprinting Key Areas of Work and Accountability:** Overview checklists for key areas (e.g., Career goals, Service, Family, Relationships, Community, Health, Financial resources, Creative expression; within job: Team morale, Processes, Timelines, Staff issues). Value is affirming areas are OK or need change.

**The More Novel the Situation, the More Control Required:** Unfamiliarity demands external checklists (e.g., prescribed procedures, new software, new job responsibilities). Use until familiar (e.g., checklist of new responsibilities during business restructuring).

**Checklists at All Levels:** Create any checklist as needed (e.g., "Core Life Values," "Things to Take Camping," "Potential Holiday Gifts," "Job Areas of Responsibility," "Exercise Regimens," "Travel Checklist," "Weekly Review," "Training Program Components," "Key Clients," "People to Stay in Touch With," "Year-end Activities," "Personal Development," "Jokes"). Capability to instantly make and use accessible checklists is core to high-performance self-management.
